entries.title: Jenny Holzer, Inflammatory Essays
text: Texts of exactly one hundred words that Jenny Holzer pasted up around Manhattan between 1979 and 1982. She drew on speeches by Mao, Lenin, Emma Goldman, Hitler and Trotsky and pressed every text into one form: twenty lines of italic capitals on a square sheet of coloured paper, unsigned. By remaining anonymous she “allows the reader to assess ideologies separated from personality”.
The format does the levelling. Every voice gets the same typeface, the same length and the same square.
facts: What it is: Jenny Holzer's one-hundred-word texts, 1979–82, originally printed on coloured paper and posted around downtown Manhattan (MASS MoCA, 'About the Texts', 2019, https://massmoca.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/Holzer_AboutTheTexts_2019.pdf).

Chat: the texts were reworked from Mao, Lenin, Goldman, Hitler and Trotsky. Confirmed by Artsy: the reading list of the Whitney's independent study programme included speeches by Mao Zedong, Vladimir Lenin, Emma Goldman, Adolf Hitler and Leon Trotsky, which Holzer began transforming into the essays (https://www.artsy.net/artist-series/jenny-holzer-inflammatory-essays).

Chat: each was forced into a fixed format, 100 words, 20 lines, italic capitals, coloured square paper, unsigned. Confirmed by Artsy: 100 words, 'formatted in capital, italicized letters, divided into 20 lines', on colourful square paper, left 'intentionally unsigned and unauthored' (https://www.artsy.net/artist-series/jenny-holzer-inflammatory-essays).

Chat: the anonymity lets readers judge an ideology separately from the personality behind it. Confirmed by MASS MoCA: by remaining anonymous, Holzer 'allows the reader to assess ideologies separated from personality' (https://massmoca.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/Holzer_AboutTheTexts_2019.pdf).

Dates differ: Artsy gives 1977–82; MASS MoCA and the Centre Pompidou give 1979–82 (https://www.artsy.net/artist-series/jenny-holzer-inflammatory-essays; https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/ressources/oeuvre/cyn9xxL).

Centre Pompidou set, AM 1988-542, gift of the artist 1988: offset print on coloured papers, 43.3 x 43.3 cm, 'hundred-word, twenty-line essays' (https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/ressources/oeuvre/cyn9xxL).

Seen in the image: a gallery wall covered floor to ceiling with square sheets in vertical columns of orange, yellow, turquoise, beige, magenta and pink, each sheet filled with lines of small dark text (manifest).

entries.title: Hans Haacke, DER BEVÖLKERUNG
text: Hans Haacke's work in a courtyard of the Reichstag in Berlin, installed in 2000: the words DER BEVÖLKERUNG, to the population, in the lettering Peter Behrens designed for the inscription DEM DEUTSCHEN VOLKE, to the German people, placed on the building in 1916. “Bevölkerung” includes everyone who lives in the country. Parliament let it stand by 260 votes to 258.
Marked as a lead on one point: the reference chat says one word was changed. It is more than that, since “Deutschen” is dropped as well.
facts: What it is: Hans Haacke's work, commissioned and installed in 2000 in the north courtyard of the Reichstag building, Berlin: a 21 x 7 metre trough from whose centre the words 'DER BEVÖLKERUNG' rise; members of the Bundestag deposit soil from their constituencies in it (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Der_Bev%C3%B6lkerung).

Chat: it reuses Peter Behrens' lettering from 'Dem Deutschen Volke'. Confirmed by Wikipedia: the title refers to the 1916 inscription 'DEM DEUTSCHEN VOLKE', underscored by 'the same lettering designed by Peter Behrens' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Der_Bev%C3%B6lkerung).

Chat: it swaps 'Volk' for 'Bevölkerung', meaning everyone who lives in the country. Confirmed by Wikipedia: 'the latter includes all people who live in a country' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Der_Bev%C3%B6lkerung).

Chat: the Bundestag approved it by 260 votes to 258. Confirmed by WSWS, 14 April 2000: on 5 April deputies voted 'by 260 to 258 in favour' of the installation. Wikipedia and the work's own site record it as a cross-party motion against the work, rejected 260 to 258 (258 for the motion, 260 against, 31 abstentions) (https://www.wsws.org/en/articles/2000/04/haac-a14.html; https://derbevoelkerung.de/en/debate/).

Chat: 'Same font, one word changed.' Not found on the pages read, and the inscriptions as quoted there differ by more than one word: 'DEM DEUTSCHEN VOLKE' and 'DER BEVÖLKERUNG', with the article changed and 'DEUTSCHEN' dropped (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Der_Bev%C3%B6lkerung).
WSWS: the Nazis favoured the word 'Volk' to stress an exclusive, nationalist notion of German identity (https://www.wsws.org/en/articles/2000/04/haac-a14.html).
Seen in the image: a rectangular planted bed in a paved courtyard seen from above, with the white letters 'DER BEVÖLKERUNG' set across the greenery and a young tree beside them (manifest).

images.caption: Geoprofi Lars, courtyard of the Reichstag with Hans Haacke's DER BEVÖLKERUNG, 5 May 2019. CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

entries.creator: Hans Haacke
entries.rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (photograph, Geoprofi Lars, Wikimedia Commons)

confidence.note: Behrens lettering, the Volk/Bevölkerung swap and the 260 to 258 vote confirmed on Wikipedia, WSWS and derbevoelkerung.de; 'one word changed' not supported.

entries.title: Errol Morris, the typeface experiment in The New York Times
text: In 2012 readers of the New York Times took a quiz in which one passage appeared in one of six typefaces, assigned at random: Baskerville, Computer Modern, Georgia, Helvetica, Comic Sans, Trebuchet. About 45,000 people answered. “Comic Sans has the lowest rate of agreement.” Morris concluded that a typeface “can subtly influence us to believe that a sentence is true”.
The effect is small. The headline result was Baskerville's advantage of about 1.5 per cent, and in David Dunning's analysis Comic Sans is only marginally significant.
facts: What it is: a passage from David Deutsch's 'The Beginning of Infinity' embedded in a Times quiz, 'Are You an Optimist or a Pessimist?', each reader seeing it in one randomly assigned typeface; reported in Errol Morris's two-part essay 'Hear, All Ye People; Hearken, O Earth', The New York Times Opinionator, 8 and 9 August 2012; about 45,000 people took the quiz (https://archive.nytimes.com/opinionator.blogs.nytimes.com/2012/08/08/hear-all-ye-people-hearken-o-earth/).

Chat: Comic Sans was compared with Baskerville, Helvetica, Georgia, Trebuchet and Computer Modern. Confirmed by Part 1: 'Baskerville, Computer Modern, Georgia, Helvetica, Comic Sans and Trebuchet' (https://archive.nytimes.com/opinionator.blogs.nytimes.com/2012/08/08/hear-all-ye-people-hearken-o-earth/).

Chat: Comic Sans made readers slightly less likely to believe a statement was true. Confirmed by Part 1: 'Comic Sans has the lowest rate of agreement', and by slwoods.co.uk, which reports the same comparison (https://archive.nytimes.com/opinionator.blogs.nytimes.com/2012/08/08/hear-all-ye-people-hearken-o-earth/; https://www.slwoods.co.uk/?p=14668).

Doubt: the headline result was Baskerville's advantage (about 1.5 per cent); in David Dunning's analysis printed in Part 2, Comic Sans is only 'marginally' significant, and on a plain agree/disagree count no typeface difference survives the correction for chance (https://archive.nytimes.com/opinionator.blogs.nytimes.com/2012/08/09/hear-all-ye-people-hearken-o-earth-part-2/).
Morris: a typeface 'can subtly influence us to believe that a sentence is true' (https://archive.nytimes.com/opinionator.blogs.nytimes.com/2012/08/09/hear-all-ye-people-hearken-o-earth-part-2/).

Morris on Comic Sans: its conscious awareness promotes, among some people, 'contempt and summary dismissal' (https://archive.nytimes.com/opinionator.blogs.nytimes.com/2012/08/08/hear-all-ye-people-hearken-o-earth/).
Seen in the image: a stacked bar chart headed 'Agreement', one bar per typeface; the Comic Sans bar is the lowest (4523), Helvetica the highest (4715), Baskerville 4703 (manifest).

images.caption: Benjamin Berman for Errol Morris, 'Agreement' by typeface, The New York Times Opinionator, 8 August 2012. Credited 'Benjamin Berman'; no licence stated.

entries.title: Ibo Omari, #PaintBack
text: Since 2015 the Berlin graffiti artist and shop owner Ibo Omari and a group of sprayers have painted over swastikas on walls, turning them into “flowers, cars and animals”. By 2017 they had transformed about 25, and the idea had been copied in Hamburg, Kiel and Bremen. He publishes templates so that anyone can do the same.
The symbol is not removed. It is drawn on until it is something else. The motto: “Answering messages of hate with love & art”.
facts: What it is: Berlin graffiti artist and shop owner Ibo Omari and a group of graffiti artists paint over swastikas into other images; he started the project in 2015 after a man came into his shop for spray paint to cover a swastika (Reuters, Michelle Martin, 19 August 2017, https://uk.news.yahoo.com/graffiti-activists-berlin-turn-nazi-symbols-art-104830589.html).

Chat: the group turns swastika graffiti into animals, flowers and other playful images. Confirmed by Reuters: the Nazi symbols become 'colourful artwork such as flowers, cars and animals'; and by HuffPost on Yahoo: 'animals, flowers and other fun images' (https://uk.news.yahoo.com/graffiti-activists-berlin-turn-nazi-symbols-art-104830589.html; https://www.yahoo.com/news/graffiti-artists-transforming-swastikas-buildings-163721560.html).

Chat: it publishes templates so anyone can do the same. Confirmed by Laughing Squid (Lori Dorn, 9 January 2018): Omari 'has also created templates for others to do the same'. Reuters does not mention templates (https://laughingsquid.com/swastika-graffiti-transformed-into-street-art/).

Laughing Squid names his association, Die kulturellen Erben e.V., and the tagline 'Answering messages of hate with love & art' (https://laughingsquid.com/swastika-graffiti-transformed-into-street-art/).

Reuters: around 25 swastikas transformed so far; the 'PaintBack' initiative copied in Hamburg, Kiel and Bremen (https://uk.news.yahoo.com/graffiti-activists-berlin-turn-nazi-symbols-art-104830589.html).
Seen in the image: black spray-painted lines on a white wall forming a running cartoon figure with a dark bob haircut, lines across the body and a skirt; no swastika is visible as such (manifest).
No credit or rights statement for the image on the source page (manifest).

images.caption: #PaintBack, a swastika painted over into a running figure, Berlin, as shown on Laughing Squid, 9 January 2018. No credit or rights statement on the page.

entries.title: Roel Nieskens, Sans Bullshit Sans
text: A font by the Dutch developer Roel Nieskens, built on the open-source Droid Sans. Type a buzzword from its list and the font replaces it with a censorship bar in the manner of Comic Sans. There is no script behind it, only “plain ol' OpenType font technology”: the ligature feature that normally joins an f to an i.
The reference chat proposes the same trick with fascist slogans as the word list: a typeface that refuses to set certain words.
facts: What it is: a font and the post that builds it, 'Sans Bullshit Sans: leveraging the synergy of ligatures', Pixelambacht, 26 February 2015, the site of Roel Nieskens, font-and-frontend developer in the Netherlands (https://pixelambacht.nl/2015/sans-bullshit-sans/).

Chat: built on Droid Sans. Confirmed: the author chose 'the open source font Droid Sans' because its Apache licence allows it to be modified and redistributed (https://pixelambacht.nl/2015/sans-bullshit-sans/).

Chat: it uses only OpenType ligatures, no CSS or JavaScript. Confirmed: 'we won't be using CSS or JavaScript for this, but plain ol' OpenType font technology' (https://pixelambacht.nl/2015/sans-bullshit-sans/).

Chat: listed buzzwords are replaced with a Comic Sans-styled censorship bar. Confirmed: 'every buzzword will be replaced by a Comic Sans-styled censorship bar'; the list is linked to an ngenworks post of buzzwords (https://pixelambacht.nl/2015/sans-bullshit-sans/).
The chat's own use of it: the same trick with fascist slogans as the word list. A proposal, not a claim about the work (manifest).
Doubt: the post states no licence for Sans Bullshit Sans itself or for its images; Droid Sans' Apache licence is the only one named (https://pixelambacht.nl/2015/sans-bullshit-sans/).

Seen in the image: a sentence set in a plain sans in which several words are covered by small black hand-drawn bars reading 'b.s.', 'bullshit' and 'bullfuckingshit'; the picture is the last frame of the animated demonstration on the post (manifest).

images.caption: Roel Nieskens, Sans Bullshit Sans in use, last frame of the animated demonstration, Pixelambacht, 26 February 2015. No licence stated for the image.

source.label: Pixelambacht, 'Sans Bullshit Sans: leveraging the synergy of ligatures', 26 February 2015

entries.title: Archigraphiæ. Rationalist Lettering and Architecture in Fascist Rome
text: A research project and summer school of the Swiss art school ECAL with ISIA Urbino, held in Rome in 2018, and the book that followed in 2020. Students recorded and digitised the geometric lettering on the regime's buildings to show how small details turn “a neutral geometrical font into a very Italian-style fascist symbol”, and so to “deconstruct the mechanisms” of this piece of propaganda.
The book includes Jonathan Pierini's essay “For the Liberation of Rationalist Lettering”. For this project it is the method to follow before any letter is swapped: draw the original first.
facts: What it is: a research project and summer school at the Swiss Institute in Rome, 'Research project (2018)', with ECAL MA in Type Design and ISIA Urbino students, project leaders Matthieu Cortat, Davide Fornari and Jonathan Pierini; book edited by Cortat and Fornari, Renens: ECAL 2020 (https://ecal.ch/en/feed/projects/5098/archigraphi-rationalist-lettering-and-architecture-in-fascist-rome/).
Chat: ECAL + ISIA Urbino, 2018. Confirmed by the ECAL page above (https://ecal.ch/en/feed/projects/5098/archigraphi-rationalist-lettering-and-architecture-in-fascist-rome/).

Chat: the project mapped the geometric sans-serif lettering of Fascist Rome to take apart how it served propaganda. Confirmed: original designs were digitised to show how small elements turn 'a neutral geometrical font into a very Italian-style fascist symbol', and 'By mapping this conspicuous feature of fascist propaganda' the school aimed to 'deconstruct the mechanisms' behind it (https://ecal.ch/en/feed/projects/5098/archigraphi-rationalist-lettering-and-architecture-in-fascist-rome/).

Chat: the book includes Jonathan Pierini's essay 'For the Liberation of Rationalist Lettering'. Confirmed by a book-spread photograph on the ECAL page (© ECAL / Jimmy Rachez) showing that heading with his name; the page's text lists Pierini among the contributors but gives no essay titles (https://ecal.ch/en/feed/projects/5098/archigraphi-rationalist-lettering-and-architecture-in-fascist-rome/).

Book record: Renens, ECAL, December 2020, ISBN 9782970135685, bilingual English and Italian (HES-SO repository record of Matthieu Cortat's chapter 'Scripta Manent', https://arodes.hes-so.ch/record/7229).

The chat's own use of it: the reference for digitising the original letterforms before swapping them; the ECAL page says original designs 'were digitised to reveal their construction' (https://ecal.ch/en/feed/projects/5098/archigraphi-rationalist-lettering-and-architecture-in-fascist-rome/).

Seen in the image: an open book; on the left a black-and-white close-up of carved capital letters standing in relief; on the right the heading 'FOR THE LIBERATION OF RATIONALIST LETTERING', the name 'JONATHAN PIERINI' and a column of text (manifest).

images.caption: Spread from Archigraphiæ (ECAL, 2020) opening Jonathan Pierini's essay. © ECAL / Jimmy Rachez; ECAL project page.

entries.title: The Communist Manifesto (In Comic Sans)
text: A print-on-demand edition of the Communist Manifesto from 2020 whose back cover calls it “one of the most influential texts in history”, set “in the most revolutionary fonts: comic sans”. The cover itself is not even in Comic Sans, and its hammer and sickle look drawn in Microsoft Paint. The library that catalogues it calls it “a meme not turned into, but being, a book itself”. Who produced it “is not apparent”.
Marked as a lead on one point: the reference chat read it as affectionate self-irony, while the catalogue speaks of trolling.
facts: What it is: a print-on-demand reprint of the Manifesto on Lulu, 2020, ISBN 9781678123635, paperback, 66 pages, catalogued by apod.li, Library of Artistic Print on Demand; who produced it 'is not apparent', it was uploaded through a Lulu store named 'john walmart' (https://apod.li/the-communist-manifesto-in-comic-sans).

Chat: the back cover calls it one of history's most influential texts, set in Comic Sans as 'the most revolutionary font'. Confirmed, quoting the back cover: 'one of the most influential texts in history', 'in the most revolutionary fonts: comic sans' (plural 'fonts') (https://apod.li/the-communist-manifesto-in-comic-sans).
Chat: the cover isn't actually set in Comic Sans. Confirmed: 'the font used on the book cover isn't even the infamous Comic Sans' (https://apod.li/the-communist-manifesto-in-comic-sans).

Chat: the front and back illustrations look hand-drawn in Microsoft Paint. Confirmed: the illustrations on the front and back covers were 'hand-drawn in what seems to be Microsoft Paint' (https://apod.li/the-communist-manifesto-in-comic-sans).
Chat: less a book turned into a meme than a meme that happens to be a book. Confirmed: 'a meme not turned into, but being, a book itself' (https://apod.li/the-communist-manifesto-in-comic-sans).

Chat: the edition is 'self-ironic and affectionate rather than debunking'. Not found on apod.li, which speaks of 'trolling alterations' and says the back cover mocks the Manifesto's final slogan and Marx's biography (https://apod.li/the-communist-manifesto-in-comic-sans).

Seen in the image: a red paperback lying flat; on the cover the title 'The Communist Manifesto (In Comic Sans)' in white rounded letters, a yellow hand-drawn hammer and sickle, and 'By Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels' (manifest).

images.caption: The Communist Manifesto (In Comic Sans), Lulu, 2020, photographed by apod.li. CC BY-SA, per the apod.li imprint.

entries.title: Andrea Lo Giudice, A + G
text: A project by Andrea Lo Giudice for the Short Theatre festival in Rome, September 2022. Phosphorescent pigment is applied to some letters of the fascist inscriptions carved on a building. In the dark those letters give back the daylight they have stored, and “new phrases will emerge”. In the picture, the inscription “NECESSARIO VINCERE / PIÙ NECESSARIO COMBATTERE” glows with the letters A, M, A, R, E: amare, to love.
The work lasts until the weather wears it off. The picture is a render, not a photograph of the work as made.
facts: What it is: a site-specific project of ephemeral interventions on Fascist-era buildings in Rome; its first phase, at Short Theatre 2022 (6–18 September, from dusk), transformed the facade of WEGIL, formerly the Littorio Italian Youth House (https://www.shorttheatre.org/en/eventi/andrea-lo-giudice/).

Chat: he applies phosphorescent pigment to selected letters of fascist inscriptions on Rome's buildings. Confirmed: natural phosphorescent pigments, previously protected by a cyclododecane film, applied to 'some letters of the fascist inscriptions' (https://www.shorttheatre.org/en/eventi/andrea-lo-giudice/).

Chat: so new phrases appear in the dark. Confirmed: in the dark the pigment releases accumulated daylight and 'new phrases will emerge' from the inscriptions engraved in the marble (https://www.shorttheatre.org/en/eventi/andrea-lo-giudice/).

Chat: the work degrades naturally over time. Confirmed: visible for a limited time, depending on atmospheric agents, 'until its natural deterioration' (https://www.shorttheatre.org/en/eventi/andrea-lo-giudice/).

The page calls it a 'poetic resemantization' of the letters; materials phosphorescent pigments, cellulose pulp and cyclododecane film; produced with restorers Michela Gottardo and Francesca Gottardo (https://www.shorttheatre.org/en/eventi/andrea-lo-giudice/).
Doubt: the picture is a render (its file name on the page reads 'render-dal-basso'), not a photograph of the realised work (manifest).

Seen in the image: a stone-clad tower seen from below at night; in the inscription 'NECESSARIO VINCERE / PIÙ NECESSARIO COMBATTERE' the letters A, M, A, R, E glow pale blue, and a few letters glow in a line near the top (manifest).

entries.title: Rada Musikarat, Hitler Archive: The Unpublished Design
text: A student project at the University of the Arts London. Rada Musikarat collected Nazi newspapers, posters and other propaganda, “changed all the blackletter font into Futura”, printed the results and put them in an archive box, “to parody the context of the original text”. Her premise is that Hitler disliked blackletter and liked Futura; a slide on her page cites the party's decree of 1941 against Fraktur.

It is the closest precedent found for swapping the typeface of fascist material. Marked as a lead on one point: the reference chat called the swap “ironic rather than funny”, which her post does not say.
facts: What it is: a student project on the maker's University of the Arts London course blog, post 'Methods of Translating', week 3, filed under Unit1, dated 31 January 2023 (https://rada.myblog.arts.ac.uk/2023/01/31/methods-of-translating-week3/).

Chat: she collected newspapers, posters and other Nazi propaganda material and changed all the blackletter into Futura. Confirmed by the post above: she collected newspapers, posters and other Nazi propaganda and 'changed all the blackletter font into Futura' (https://rada.myblog.arts.ac.uk/2023/01/31/methods-of-translating-week3/).

Chat: she printed them and presented them in an archive box called 'Hitler Archive: The Unpublished Design'. Confirmed by the post above, which gives the box that title and calls the format 'an archive box' (https://rada.myblog.arts.ac.uk/2023/01/31/methods-of-translating-week3/).

Chat: 'The swap is ironic rather than funny'. Not found as worded on the post above: it says the box is meant 'to parody the context of the original text' (https://rada.myblog.arts.ac.uk/2023/01/31/methods-of-translating-week3/).

Chat: it plays on Hitler's own 1941 ban on Fraktur. Only partly found: the post's text gives the premise 'Hitler didn't like blackletter and actually like Futura'; the first slide on the same page reproduces a spread from Ruben Pater, 'The Politics of Design', headed 'Hitler Did Not Like Blackletter', which cites the NSDAP decree of 1941 (https://rada.myblog.arts.ac.uk/2023/01/31/methods-of-translating-week3/).

Seen in the image: a black slipcase labelled in blackletter 'Hitler Archive' and 'The unpublished designs' (plural on the label); beside it printed sheets reset in a geometric sans, a red and white newspaper page headed 'Magdeburg' and an eagle-and-swastika sign lettered 'NSDAP' (manifest).
No rights statement on the source page (manifest).

entries.title: Tommy Robinson and Peter McLoughlin, Manifesto: a cover in Comic Sans
text: The cover of a 2024 book by the British far-right activist who calls himself Tommy Robinson, with the title and the authors' names set in Comic Sans. It is here as a counter-example: the typeface that is supposed to make a text ridiculous sat on a book that reached number one on Amazon's British chart.

The blogger who pointed it out mocked the choice. The reference chat draws the lesson that the far right does not always treat the font as a joke; that is its conclusion, not a documented fact. Read only through reporting.
facts: What it is: the cover of 'Manifesto' (2024), a book by Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, who calls himself Tommy Robinson, written with ghost writer Peter McLoughlin. Read only in reporting about it; no site or shop of the author was opened (https://www.slwoods.co.uk/?p=14668).

Chat: the cover set its title and author names in Comic Sans. Confirmed by Steve Woods, 'Font for fascism', 16 October 2024: the title and the authors' names 'were all written in the Comic Sans font' (https://www.slwoods.co.uk/?p=14668).

Chat: 'The far right doesn't always treat the font as a joke.' This is the chat's own conclusion, not a claim a page can confirm; slwoods instead mocks the choice, citing Errol Morris on Comic Sans and 'contempt and summary dismissal' (https://www.slwoods.co.uk/?p=14668).

The book, subtitled 'Free Speech, Real Democracy, Peaceful Disobedience', reached No 1 on Amazon's UK bestseller chart before selling out; this report does not mention the font (The Guardian, Hannah Al-Othman, 10 October 2024, https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2024/oct/10/amazon-criticised-as-tommy-robinson-book-tops-chart).

Seen in the image: a white cover with a red band and a red edge strip; the names 'Peter McLoughlin' and 'Tommy Robinson' and the title 'Manifesto' in a rounded, informal letter of the Comic Sans kind; the three subtitle lines below in a plainer sans (manifest).
No rights statement for the image on the source page (manifest).
